prompt.context: An enterprise technology company that builds applications for businesses outsourced large parts of its organization, thereby reducing its employee base by 60%. Yet, they are spending $1.8B, which is $150M more than industry benchmarks. Tensions among employees are high with fears of more lay-offs, and there is immense pressure on the CEO, your client, to close the gap to industry benchmarks.
prompt.question: How would you advise the client to close the $150M gap to industry benchmarks?

clarifying_info.q: What products does the client sell or who are their customers?
clarifying_info.a: That information is unavailable. Why do you think that is relevant?

clarifying_info.q: What are the main functions within the company?
clarifying_info.a: The three main functions are Development (creates and improves products, mostly highly skilled software engineers), Support (first point of contact with customers, relays customer needs to Development, resolves basic issues or escalates complex ones), and Admin (administrative functions including HR, procurement, finance, etc.).

clarifying_info.q: What other cost categories exist beyond payroll?
clarifying_info.a: You can see the breakdown in Exhibit 1 — ask what impact you think you could have in those other categories.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost per FTE for Developers and Admin?
clarifying_info.a: Developers in high-cost locations cost $250k/FTE and in low-cost locations $100k/FTE. Admin in high-cost locations costs $200k/FTE and in low-cost locations $50k/FTE.

exhibits.title: Actual vs. Projected Spend by Category, 2014
exhibits.shows: Stacked bar chart comparing actual 2014 spend ($1,800M) versus projected industry benchmark spend ($1,650M) across five cost categories

data.Note: Numbers visible on chart bars; actual total $1,800M vs benchmark $1,650M; the gap appears concentrated in payroll (500 actual vs 500 benchmark) and software licenses (500 actual vs 450 benchmark) and hardware (450 vs 450) — candidate must interpret which bucket drives the $150M gap

exhibits.title: Employee Count by Function and Country (# FTEs)
exhibits.shows: Table of FTE counts broken down by country (India, Germany, United States, Philippines, Mexico, United Kingdom, China) and by function (Development, Support, Admin), with location type (low-cost or high-cost) indicated for each country

framework: Focus on payroll as the primary cost driver — payroll = # employees x $ salary/employee
Branch 1: Right-sizing headcount — does the client have too many employees post-outsourcing? Is further reduction possible?
Branch 2: Compensation optimization — can salaries be lowered for some or all employees, e.g., by shifting to lower-cost locations?
Branch 3: Change management costs — post-outsourcing friction (training on new processes, retention of key talent) may be inflating costs
Underlying hypothesis: The 60% headcount reduction has not yet translated into full cost savings, so identify where savings are not materializing

questions.prompt: After reviewing Exhibit 1, where does the $150M gap come from and what should the framework focus on?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate immediately identifies that payroll is the dominant cost category and the most actionable lever. The gap is $150M versus benchmarks. While other categories exist, payroll (including benefits) is the largest single line item, and the case context (outsourcing reduced headcount 60%) makes clear that projected payroll savings have not been fully realized. The framework should center on: (a) number of employees and (b) cost per employee. Other cost categories should be acknowledged but deprioritized unless the candidate can articulate a specific lever.

questions.prompt: Between Development, Support, and Admin — each currently present in 7 countries — which function(s) could be centralized to reduce payroll cost?
questions.guidance: Centralization here means consolidating dispersed employees to one location. Key evaluation factors: (1) Customer proximity requirement — Support must stay close to customers (7 countries) because it is the direct customer interface; Development does NOT need to be close to customers since Support acts as the intermediary, so Development can likely be centralized. (2) Standardization of services — some Admin functions (finance, procurement) are globally standardizable and could be centralized; others may need local presence. (3) Risks to flag — time zone challenges, availability of talent in the new central location, new regulatory requirements in destination country. A good answer concludes that Development can be centralized, some Admin (roughly 50%) can be centralized, and Support should remain distributed.

questions.prompt: The client agrees that centralizing Development and 50% of Admin staff is feasible. Using Exhibit 2, will these changes be sufficient to close the $150M gap?
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate the cost savings from shifting high-cost-location employees to low-cost locations. Key steps: identify Development and Admin FTEs in high-cost locations (Germany, US, UK), apply the cost differential, and compare to $150M target. The math yields ~$106.5M in savings, which is insufficient to close the full $150M gap. Candidate should conclude that additional levers are needed.

math.setup: Savings = (# FTEs in high-cost locations eligible to shift) x (cost differential between high-cost and low-cost)
steps: Identify high-cost countries: Germany, United States, United Kingdom
Development FTEs in high-cost locations: Germany 100 + US 300 + UK 100 = 500; all 500 can be shifted
Admin FTEs in high-cost locations: Germany 200 + US 150 + UK 70 = 420; 50% can be shifted = 210
Gap remaining: $150M - $106.5M = $43.5M — insufficient to close the full gap
math.answer: $106.5M in savings, leaving a $43.5M gap; the centralization plan alone is insufficient

questions.prompt: Given centralization cannot close the full $150M gap, how else can the client cover the remaining shortfall? What risks do you see, and what next steps do you propose?
questions.guidance: No additional quantitative analysis required. Strong candidates refer back to their original payroll framework and surface remaining levers. Key ideas include: reducing compensation rates (renegotiation, pay freezes, variable vs. fixed comp adjustments); further headcount reduction in non-critical roles; addressing outsourcing inefficiencies (if outsourced services costs are above benchmark); training and process optimization to reduce cost per employee; managing change management costs (severance, relocation) that may have been underestimated. Important insight to highlight: $106.5M (~2/3 of the gap) can be achieved by relocating — not firing — employees, which addresses the workforce anxiety directly. Risks: execution risk of large-scale relocation, talent attrition of key engineers, regulatory/employment law in destination countries, time zone and collaboration challenges, upfront transition costs (severance for those who don't relocate, relocation packages).

brainstorming.prompt: What other ideas could the client pursue to close the remaining $43.5M gap beyond centralizing Development and 50% of Admin?

categories.name: Further headcount reduction
ideas: Identify redundant roles created by overlap between outsourced and in-house teams
Review middle management layers added post-outsourcing
Consolidate duplicative functions across business units

categories.name: Compensation restructuring
ideas: Renegotiate salaries, especially for employees whose market rate has declined
Shift portion of compensation to performance-based variable pay
Introduce tiered benefits to reduce benefits cost per FTE

categories.name: Process and efficiency improvements
ideas: Streamline onboarding/training costs for new processes post-outsourcing
Automate low-complexity Support tasks to reduce Support headcount over time
Improve handoff protocols between Support and Development to reduce rework costs

categories.name: Outsourced services optimization
ideas: Renegotiate vendor contracts for outsourced services
Repatriate select outsourced functions if in-house cost is now lower
Audit scope creep in outsourcing agreements

categories.name: Change management cost reduction
ideas: Reduce severance liability by offering relocation instead of termination
Invest in targeted retention bonuses for key talent to avoid costly attrition and rehiring
Standardize global HR and procurement processes to reduce Admin cost

categories.name: Transition / one-time costs to manage
ideas: Plan for productivity dip during transition period
Assess regulatory requirements (e.g. works councils in Germany, UK employment law)

recommendation: Centralize the Development function (500 high-cost FTEs shifted to low-cost locations) and 50% of Admin (210 FTEs shifted), generating approximately $106.5M in savings — roughly two-thirds of the $150M gap — primarily through relocation rather than layoffs, which directly addresses workforce anxiety
Pursue supplementary levers to close the remaining ~$43.5M gap, including compensation restructuring, headcount optimization in non-critical roles, and outsourced services contract renegotiation
risks: Talent attrition risk: skilled software engineers may leave rather than relocate, eroding the Development team
Regulatory and employment law complexity in high-cost countries (Germany works councils, UK employment protections) could increase severance costs and slow execution
Time zone and collaboration challenges from a more centralized but geographically distant Development team
Upfront transition costs (relocation packages, severance for non-relocating employees) could offset near-term savings
Employee morale and productivity may decline during the transition, delaying cost realization
next_steps: Collect granular data on Development FTE counts by location and willingness to relocate
Engage legal counsel in Germany, US, and UK to assess employment law constraints and estimate transition costs
Identify target central location(s) for Development based on talent availability, cost, and time zone coverage
Model sensitivity of savings to attrition rates among high-cost-location developers
Design change management program to communicate relocation plan and reduce workforce anxiety
